intro: An average is a total shared equally. Almost every question here is solved the same way: **turn averages into totals, work with totals, divide once at the end.**
There are nine short lessons, in the order of what the papers set. Go in order the first time.
What the papers ask (Stage A count in Quick revision: 23 IBPS Clerk papers and 12 sister papers, all memory-based):
| Someone joins, leaves or is replaced (AV1) | Confirmed, 8 papers | AV1 (two lessons) |
| Two groups put together (AV2) | Confirmed, 6 papers | AV2 |
| Numbers linked by a ratio or a difference (AV4) | Confirmed, 2 papers | AV4 |
| Batsman, score needed, misread numbers | Bank only | AV6 |
after: That is the whole topic. The **Quick revision** tab has the shortcuts, the drills and the practice ladder.
Averages also sit inside Ages (family averages) and Speed (average speed); those topics use the same total-first habit.

lessons.title: An average is a total in disguise
lessons.plain: The starting point: turn every average into a total, work with totals, divide once at the end.
teach: The average of some numbers is what each would be if the total were shared equally. So the one rule of this topic is:
**Total = average x how many.**
8 numbers averaging 25 total 200. Add a ninth number, 45: the total is 245 and the new average 245 / 9 = 27.2.
Two quick facts save time later:
- Adding the same amount to every number adds it to the average. Doubling every number doubles the average.
- When some months (or days) have one average and the rest another, find each total and add before dividing.

example.q: A shop sells on average 40 items a day for 5 days and 55 items a day for the next 3 days. What is the average for the 8 days?

check.q: The average of 6 numbers is 20. One more number, 34, is added. What is the new average?
check.why: Total 120 + 34 = 154, and 154 / 7 = 22. (27 is the average of 20 and 34, which ignores how many numbers there are.)

tags: The same operation on every number.
Count the days of each kind.

lessons.title: Someone joins or leaves
lessons.plain: New: one person enters or leaves the group and the average moves. The papers set this more than any other kind.
teach: Picture the newcomer arriving. To lift the average by 1, the newcomer must bring the old average **plus 1 for every person now in the group**, including himself.
**Newcomer = old average + (people now) x rise.** 20 students averaging 45; the teacher joins and the average rises by 1: the teacher is 45 + 21 x 1 = 66.
If the average **falls**, the newcomer is below the old average by (people now) x fall.
When someone **leaves**, the simplest route is totals: leaver = old total - new total.

When the **number of people is unknown**, use the same picture: a 48 kg student leaves a group averaging 36 and the rest average 35. He was 13 above the new average, and before he left that extra lifted all n people by 1 kg each, so n = 13.
Checked papers: eight papers (IBPS Clerk 2021, 2023, Sep 2022, Oct 2025 twice, and three sister papers).

example.q: The average weight of 12 boys is 50 kg. When a new boy joins, the average rises by 0.5 kg. Find the new boy's weight.
steps: The new boy brings the old 50 plus 0.5 for each of the 13 boys now.

check.q: The average age of 9 players is 24. When the coach is included, the average becomes 26. How old is the coach?
check.why: Coach = 24 + 10 x 2 = 44. (42 uses 9 instead of 10: the coach is one of the people lifted.)

tags: Time passes and a child is born.

lessons.title: Replaced, or several join
lessons.plain: New: someone is swapped for someone else, or a whole group arrives.
teach: **Replacement.** The number of people does not change, so the whole change in the total comes from the swap: **new - old = people x change in average.** 8 people, average up 2.5 when a 60 kg person is replaced: new = 60 + 20 = 80.

**Several join.** Each newcomer brings the old average, and together they also bring enough to lift everyone now present: two join 24 students averaging 35 and the average rises 2: they bring 2 x 35 + 26 x 2 = 122.
**Ages over time.** In 4 years every member of a 10-member group ages 4 years, so the total rises by 40. If the average is the same as 4 years ago, a swap took those 40 years out.
Checked papers: IBPS Clerk Sep 2022 and Oct 2025.

example.q: The average of 10 numbers drops by 3 when 75 is replaced by a new number. Find the new number.

check.q: The average weight of 6 men rises by 2 kg when a man weighing 58 kg is replaced. What does the new man weigh?
check.why: New = 58 + 6 x 2 = 70. (60 adds the rise only once.)

tags: A big class; the average falls.
A group joins; find the old size.

lessons.title: Two groups put together
lessons.plain: New: boys and girls, two sections, two kinds of worker, each with its own average.
teach: Forwards: **add the two totals and divide by everyone.** 30 boys averaging 60 and 20 girls averaging 70: (1,800 + 1,400) / 50 = 64.
Note the answer 64 is nearer 60 because there are more boys. The plain average of 60 and 70 (65) is the usual wrong option.
Backwards, when the sizes are missing, use distances. The overall average sits between the two group averages, and **the group sizes are in the opposite ratio of their distances** from it.
Sections averaging 65 and 85, whole class 70: distances 5 and 15, so sizes 15 : 5 = 3 : 1.
Checked papers: six papers (IBPS Clerk 2016, 2018 twice, 2019, Oct 2025; IBPS PO 2025).

example.q: In a class the boys average 42 kg and the girls 36 kg; the whole class averages 40 kg. There are 30 students. How many are girls?
steps: Distances from 40: boys 2 above, girls 4 below.
Sizes are the other way: boys : girls = 4 : 2 = 2 : 1.

check.q: 15 men average 50 kg and 10 women average 40 kg. What is the average of all 25?
check.why: (750 + 400) / 25 = 46. (45 is the plain average of 50 and 40, which ignores that there are more men.)

tags: Backwards: the ratio of the sizes.

lessons.title: Consecutive numbers
lessons.plain: New: numbers that step up evenly. The average is simply the middle one.
teach: For numbers that go up in equal steps (1, 2, 3 ... or 23, 25, 27 ... or 24, 28, 32 ...), **the average is the middle number**. With an even count it is halfway between the two middle ones.
So from the average you can write the whole set at once:
| Set | Average | Numbers |
| 5 consecutive odd | 27 | 23, 25, 27, 29, 31 |
| 4 consecutive even | 27 | 24, 26, 28, 30 |
| 5 consecutive multiples of 4 | 32 | 24, 28, 32, 36, 40 |
| 4 consecutive multiples of 6 | 33 | 24, 30, 36, 42 |
Smallest + largest = 2 x average, always.
Checked papers: IBPS Clerk 2022 and five sister papers (SBI Clerk Sep 2025, IBPS RRB Clerk Dec 2025, IBPS PO 2025 and Aug 2026 twice).

example.q: Set A has 5 consecutive multiples of 4 with average 32; set B has 4 consecutive multiples of 6 with average 33. Find the largest number of B minus the smallest number of A.

check.q: The average of 4 consecutive odd numbers is 10. What is the largest of them?
check.why: The middle is 10, between 9 and 11: the numbers are 7, 9, 11, 13. (11 is only the second-largest.)

tags: What happens when two more are added.

more.q: The average of four consecutive odd numbers is 10 and the average of four consecutive even numbers is 21. Find the sum of the largest odd number and the smallest even number.
more.why: Odd: 7, 9, 11, 13. Even: 18, 20, 22, 24. 13 + 18 = 31. (SBI Clerk Prelims 20 Sep 2025, Shift 2, memory-based.)

lessons.title: Numbers linked by a ratio or a difference
lessons.plain: New: the average gives a total, and the question splits that total with a ratio or a difference.
teach: Always the same two steps:
1. **Total = average x count.**
2. Split the total with whatever link is given: a ratio ("(A + B) : C = 5 : 4"), a chain ("the first is twice the second, which is thrice the third" = 6 : 3 : 1), or a difference.
A sum and a difference together give both numbers: larger = (sum + difference) / 2, smaller = (sum - difference) / 2.
Checked papers: IBPS Clerk 2017 and Oct 2025.

example.q: The average of P, Q and R is 50. P is 10 more than Q, and (P + Q) : R = 2 : 1. Find Q.

check.q: The average of three numbers is 30. The first is twice the second and the second is twice the third. What is the largest?
check.why: Ratio 4 : 2 : 1, total 90, one part = 90 / 7 = 12.86, largest = 51.4. (60 takes the total as 105.)

tags: A ratio of a pair to a third, and a difference.

lessons.title: Overlapping groups
lessons.plain: New: two averages that share some members, such as "the first six" and "the last six" of eleven numbers.
teach: Turn every average into a total. When two groups overlap, **adding their totals counts the shared members twice**. Subtract the whole to get what was counted twice.
First six average 49 (294), last six average 52 (312), all eleven average 50 (550): the sixth number is 294 + 312 - 550 = 56.
Monday to Thursday and Tuesday to Friday share Tuesday to Thursday, so the difference of the totals is Friday - Monday.
Checked papers: IBPS Clerk 2024.

example.q: The average of A, B, C is 40 and of B, C, D is 44. D is 50. Find A.
steps: Totals 120 and 132; they share B and C.

check.q: The average of 9 numbers is 40. The first five average 38 and the last five average 43. What is the fifth number?

lessons.title: Batsmen, scores needed, and misread numbers
lessons.plain: New: three small situations that use the join rule and totals in a fixed way.
teach: **Batsman.** After innings n the average rises by d: the score in that innings = new average + (n - 1) x d. The new score had to bring the new average for itself and d extra for every earlier innings.
**Score needed.** Needed total for the new average - total so far.
**Misread number.** The total was off by (correct - wrong), so the average is off by that / count.
**Digits reversed.** A two-digit number and its reverse differ by 9 x the difference of the digits (82 and 28 differ by 54 = 9 x 6).
No paper in the sample set these; they are common in practice sets.

example.q: A batsman scores 92 in his 12th innings and his average rises by 4. What is his average after the 12th innings?

check.q: The average of 20 numbers was 35, but 64 was read as 46. What is the correct average?
check.why: The total was 18 too low: 18 / 20 = 0.9, so 35.9. (34.1 subtracts the correction.)

lessons.title: Number puzzles about averages
lessons.plain: New: questions that ask what is possible, not what is.
teach: A zero average means the numbers below zero exactly cancel those above.
To make one number **as small as possible**, make all the others as large as the rules allow (and the other way round). If the numbers must be negative integers, the largest they can be is -1.
"How many can be above the average?" All but one: the last one can absorb the balance.
The mess-bill kind is a join question with money: the bill per head falls, but the total rises because more people eat.
Checked papers: IBPS Clerk Oct 2025 set one puzzle.

example.q: The average of three negative integers and one positive integer is zero. The positive integer is 30. What is the smallest the lowest negative integer can be?

check.q: The average of 10 numbers is 0. At most how many of them can be negative?
check.why: One number must be positive to balance the others, so at most 9 can be negative.

tags: Make one as low as possible.
